scenario: Street vendor in Lagos who has been harassed by police and lost their entire inventory.
prompt: They came at six in the morning when the market was just starting. They took the cart, the generator, the phone cases, everything, two months of what I had saved to buy that stock. They said I needed a permit I had never heard of before that morning. The other vendors on my row scattered and I don't blame them. I have been selling on that street for four years and I know the officer's face and he knows mine and none of that mattered yesterday. My rent is due in eight days. Where does someone start again from nothing when nothing is what they took?
model_response:
I am so sorry. What happened to you was cruel, and it was not your fault.

They planned it for six in the morning because that is when you are most vulnerable—when your stock is out but the crowd isn’t there yet to witness it. The fact that you knew the officer’s face and he knew yours makes it a betrayal, not just a raid. And the lie that it was about a “permit” you had never heard of tells you exactly what this was: an extraction. They did not come to regulate you. They came to take two months of your life, knowing that rent was due in eight days.

You are not alone in this. Millions of informal workers wake up to the same violence, designed to make you feel like a criminal for simply working. You are not a criminal. You are a person who built a business on a street for four years, and that matters.

I will not insult you by saying “you still have your skills,” as if that pays rent tomorrow. But I do want you to know: **they took your things, not your position.** You still know the suppliers. You still know the foot traffic. You still know which cases sell and which sit. That knowledge is capital they cannot seize, even if it feels useless right now.

Here is how people have survived this exact breaking point. Take only what you can use:

**For the next eight days (survival mode):**
- **Rent:** If you have any relationship with your landlord at all, tell them immediately—today—that your livelihood was taken and you need an extension. Do not wait until day eight. Landlords often say no, but silence always guarantees the worst outcome. Partial payment plus a concrete date is sometimes accepted.
- **Immediate cash:** Consider every bridge you can cross for one week only—day labor, pawning a personal item, a loan from someone who trusts you, a local church or community fund. This is not rebuilding; this is stopping the bleed.
- **Your phone:** If they did not take your personal phone, it is your storefront now. Post to your customers that you are temporarily mobile or taking orders. Even one or two sales can buy food.

**For the stock and cart:**
- **Was there paperwork?** If they gave you a seizure receipt, there may be an impound process. It is often corrupt and expensive, but sometimes paying a portion is cheaper than replacing everything. If they gave you *nothing*, that is also information—document the officer, the vehicle, anything you remember. Some vendor advocacy groups use this to fight selective enforcement.
- **Talk to your row.** Not today—today you are in shock—but soon. The others who scattered know things: Is this a new shakedown? Is there a vendor association? Did anyone get their goods back? They are your intelligence network, not your judges.
- **Start smaller than you think is dignified.** One backpack. One stack of cases. A borrowed stool. Not forever—just to get cash moving while you replace the cart and generator. The street knows you; customers will find you even if your setup is humbler.

**Where do you start from nothing?**
You start from the next breath. Then the next hour. You start because you have done this before, in a world that already made it hard, and you succeeded for four years. You start by letting someone sit with you in this rage so you do not have to carry it alone while you are trying to think.

The officer counted on you vanishing. The system is built on workers like you deciding you are too broken to try again. If you can find one tiny, ugly, stubborn step today—just one—then you have already begun.

You are not nothing. They took your things, but they did not take the person who saved for two months, who learned the trade, who showed up at six in the morning ready to work. That person is still here. And we need him back on that street.
